summary:
Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks facing transgender visitors have sharpened sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the United States State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The same statutes operate inside Dagestan as in every other Russian region.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024 involving abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses transgender people and visible advocates as a specific category within that finding. This note sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia and separately warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, identifying the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan in particular. The same advisory states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of Interior, a requirement a visitor may encounter when moving through the republic.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He said the situation worsens year on year.
tangentialFactors:
Global Affairs Canada flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, a security condition distinct from anti-LGBT violence but shaping any movement through the region.

The North Caucasus pattern sits inside a national enforcement trend that has accelerated in volume as well as severity. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, and Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget over two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Comparable raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025).

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented at national scale. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
localsOnly:
Residents of Dagestan live under the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care, which removes the possibility of changing gender markers on Russian official documents and of accessing transition-related medical procedures anywhere in the country.

The Home Office assessment that LGBT+ people in the North Caucasus face persecution applies to people leaving the region, and its recognition of trans people and visible advocates as a specific category shapes whether a Dagestan resident can establish a claim under the refugee convention.

North Caucasus SOS reports that for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year. The reference to forced return to families indicates that family members are a recognised source of risk for residents, not only state authorities.

The UK Home Office country policy note (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Dagestan-specific court decisions, prosecutions or administrative fines under the propaganda or extremism statutes are sourced in this inventory; the enforcement evidence cited is national or drawn from other regions, and the Dagestan-specific findings rest on the Home Office assessment, the Canadian advisory and one practitioner's testimony.

The inventory does not state which areas or regions of Russia the Ministry of Interior special-permission requirement covers, or whether any part of Dagestan falls within them; that scope is unresolved here.

The 2017 to 2024 campaign documentation is attributed in the Home Office note to Chechen and North Caucasus authorities collectively; the inventory does not break out how much of that activity is attributed specifically to Dagestan authorities rather than Chechen ones, which remains unresolved.

David Isteev's assessment is a practitioner account given in exile and is not independently corroborated within this inventory. No sourced information covers the availability of medical care, documentation services or safe accommodation for transgender visitors inside Dagestan.
